growth_story.headline: Russia's income per person collapsed in the 1990s, surged with oil until 2008, then grew 1.3 percent a year through crises, sanctions and war.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1998, as the Soviet system broke up, income per person shrank by 6.2 percent a year, and the period ended with a debt default in August 1998. From 1999 to 2008 it grew 7.3 percent a year, a recovery the IMF ties partly to rising oil prices. Since 2009 growth has averaged 1.3 percent a year. The global financial crisis and the 2015 crisis each left lasting output losses, and the IMF blamed low oil prices, tight policies, sanctions and structural limits for lackluster growth before COVID-19. After the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, a war-driven economy lifted income per person by 4.4 percent in 2023 and 5.0 in 2024, but growth slowed to 1.1 in 2025 while high borrowing costs weighed on spending. Income per person was at its highest so far in 2025, yet the last decade averaged 1.9 percent a year against 2.5 in the decade before.

threads.title: Transition collapse and 1998 default
threads.text: Income per person fell almost every year from 1990 to 1998, by as much as 14.6 percent in 1992, as the old planned economy came apart. The IMF describes a huge fall in output early in the transition, ending in a loss of confidence and a debt default in August 1998.

threads.title: Oil-lifted rebound after 1999
threads.text: After the default, growth returned quickly: income per person rose 10.5 percent in 2000 and stayed above 5 percent a year through 2008. The IMF calls it Russia's first period of sustained growth and says rising oil prices gave it a further push.

threads.title: Crises that left scars
threads.text: Income per person fell 7.8 percent in 2009, and a second recession followed in 2014–15 as oil prices fell and sanctions arrived. The IMF found that output never got back to its earlier trend after either crisis, and it blamed low oil prices, tight policies, sanctions and long-standing structural limits for weak growth in the years before COVID-19.

citations.title: Russian Federation: 2020 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report
citations.quote: Both the global financial crisis (GFC) and the 2015 crisis have seen large scarring, with output never recovering to its pre-crisis trend.

citations.title: Russian Federation: 2020 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report
citations.quote: the combination of low oil prices, tight policies, sanctions, and long-standing structural constraints, led to lackluster growth

threads.title: A war-driven economy
threads.text: Sanctions after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine cut output, and income per person fell 1.1 percent that year. War-related demand then lifted growth to 4.4 percent in 2023 and 5.0 in 2024. The World Bank says this growth model is now weakening and that very low unemployment reflects labor shortages rather than broad strength.

citations.title: Global Economic Prospects: Europe and Central Asia

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Russian Federation
citations.quote: Russia’s economy remains outwardly resilient but is under increasing macro-financial pressure as the war-driven growth model weakens.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Russian Federation
citations.quote: Labor market indicators reflect war-related labor shortages rather than broad-based economic strength.

threads.title: Costly credit and sanctions
threads.text: Growth in income per person slowed to 1.1 percent in 2025. The World Bank says high borrowing costs from tight monetary policy kept weighing on household spending and business investment. It expects growth to ease further in 2026 and ties this to capacity limits, sanctions, high borrowing costs and refinery outages.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Russian Federation
citations.quote: High borrowing costs, due to tight monetary policy, continued affecting private consumption and investment.

citations.title: The World Bank in the Russian Federation: Overview
citations.quote: high borrowing costs, the impact of sanctions, and refinery outages

since_last_year.text: Growth in income per person fell from 5.0 percent in 2024 to 1.1 in 2025. The World Bank's October 2026 note says growth slowed again in the first half of 2026. High borrowing costs held back spending, and damage to energy infrastructure led to fuel rationing and higher prices.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Russian Federation
citations.quote: Real GDP growth continued decelerating, from 1 percent in 2025 to 0.6 percent year-on-year (yoy) during the first half of 2026.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Russian Federation
citations.quote: Damage to energy infrastructure have forced fuel rationing across many Russian regions, pushed domestic gasoline prices higher, and lifted headline inflation.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person at its highest level so far in 2025, after growth of 4.4 percent in 2023 and 5.0 in 2024. The World Bank calls that growth war-driven and says the tight labor market reflects labor shortages, not broad strength. It also says the authorities have chosen to limit what economic data they publish, which makes the economy hard to assess. So the peak in the data may say less about lasting gains than it seems to.
